sent.t: I'm going to tell you something that almost nobody says out loud.
There are things that a Mexican family does in a funeral, and that on the other side of the border, a funeral prohibits it.
I'm not saying it out loud.
I've been putting on a black jacket for more than 40 years, and standing next to a family that just lost someone.
I buried more than 6,000 people, and I can tell you by name and last name, at what time a Mexican family comes across a rule
that they do not understand.
It is a rule that is not written in Spanish, it is written on a graped sheet that they give you when you arrive, with a
small letter, and that almost nobody reads because at that time one is not there to read.
There it says, for example, that the chapel closes at 7, that you cannot spend the night, Que no se puede comer, que no se puede
poner música.
Y uno lo lee y piensa, pues ¿qué se puede?
Yo trabajé 25 años en funerarias del West Side de San Antonio, en la Guadalupe, en la Zarzamora, en la Commerce.
Atendí familias de Michoacán, de Jalisco, de Zacatecas, de Nuevo León.
Familias que llegaban con su olla de café de olla y su bolsa de pan dulce y que se quedaban paradas en la puerta de la
capilla, como quien llega a una casa ajena y no sabe si puede pasar.
Esa cara la tengo grabada.
Es la cara de alguien a quien le están diciendo, con mucha educación, que aquí no.
Y del otro lado, en Analco, en la casa de mi papá, la puerta nunca se cerraba.
My father, Don Refugio Navarro, opened Funerales Navarro in 1958, two blocks from the San Sebastián Temple.
I started at 13 years old, sweeping the chapel, and I learned something that is not in any regulation.
The funeral is not from the funeral home, it is from the family.
We are the ones who carry the chairs.
Today I am going to tell you nine things that are done in a Mexican funeral home and that in the United States, in most funerals,
they do not let them do it.
And I am not going to tell you so that you get angry with anyone.
I am going to tell you so that the day it is your turn, you will know what to ask and what you do not have
to accept.
because half of these things are not laws, they are customs of the funeral home and the customs are negotiated.

In a Mexican velorio, the velorio is not a visit, it is a night.
